Jean-Denis Greze, founder of @TownAI, argues AI isn't diffusing because most people aren't tinkerers: a text box isn't enough, so the product must both identify the value prop and perform the work for them.

"There's this business that rents surfboards on an island to people and then uses Town to inspect surfboards and little beach buggies, whether they've been damaged, to decide whether afterwards the person should get their deposit back."

"What makes it work there is the tinkerer... The unlock is, is there someone over there that gets AI enough to wanna tinker a solution to their problem?"

"And the problem with that is that there aren't enough tinkerers in the world, or there aren't enough people that have the time to be tinkerers to help their business. And I think that's why AI is not diffusing."

"Instead what you're doing is you're using [AI tools] as a replacement, as like a better Google search."

"If you can make a non-tinkerer into getting the same value as a tinkerer... you could be a ginormous business today because AI can solve so many business problems. You don't need more intelligence. The intelligence is there."

Jean-Denis Greze, founder of @TownAI, on the question that made him kill his first startup despite nearly $1M in first-year revenue: can you outrun the incumbents using the same technology?

"After one year, we had what I would describe as a good business pre-AI... But post-AI, this was not gonna be a venture scale company."

"We realized that the incumbents were gonna be able to use the technology to automate tax prep for their existing customers faster than we could grab market share. That's like a key thing if you're a founder you have to think about."

"Your advantage if you're a new entrant is you're faster moving, you can build a different product, you can use different go-to-market approaches, but there's a ticking clock on the wall."

"It felt for tax like we wouldn't be able to get to hundreds of millions of revenue before our competitors, the incumbents could, because you can only sell tax once a year... It's rare for people to brag about their tax prep situation."

Jean-Denis Greze, founder of @TownAI, on the question every AI app founder gets asked: what stops the big labs from crushing you?

"It is risky always to be competing with your suppliers, right? We're competing against our suppliers. So you gotta ask yourself, is that naturally the right state of the world?"

"Someone at OpenAI, at Anthropic, at Google could wake up and decide to do that. So the better answer actually is to think about our customers and what they want."

"It is our job to determine from all the AI capabilities, frontier model, open weight, what is the right thing for you as a business. And I think you can save money there, but also you can de-risk ever having made the wrong partner."

"There are companies that picked OpenAI like two years ago, and then Anthropic was better at coding for a 12-month period. And those companies had to use both because they realized to be competitive, they needed Claude."

"If you're a smart business, you really think about the neutrality of who's providing intelligence for you and who's routing."

Jean-Denis Greze was CTO of Plaid. His next startup, an AI tax product for small businesses, brought in nearly $1M in revenue its first year, and he projected $2.5 to $3M the next. He shut it down anyway.

The reason: in the age of AI, it was never going to be venture scale. Incumbents could use the same technology to automate tax prep for their existing customers faster than a startup could win market share. Tax is also sold once a year, so he had about a one-month window to pivot before the door closed.

The pivot became Town, an AI assistant that works from your email and calendar. It found product-market fit fast enough that Ben Horowitz messaged a16z's Alex Rampell to say it "changed my life."

In this conversation, Alex and Jean-Denis cover:

- How to know when to kill a business that's working on paper
- Why Town competes with OpenAI and Anthropic, the companies it buys its tokens from
- Why the "forward deployed engineer" model gets worse as AI gets better
- How a $1/month AI routine can save a restaurant thousands
- What agents mean for Amazon, advertising and the future of shopping
